notes.explains: The bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3 against the king, and that knight has no legal move at all. So taking on e5 loses a pawn outright: Black takes on e4 and there is no recapture, because the only piece that guards it cannot move. Pushing the d-pawn past instead gains space and forces the knight on c6 to find a new square.
notes.teaches: Before making a capture in the centre, check whether the piece you are counting on to recapture is pinned. A bishop pinning a knight against the king does not have to win material to matter — it removes that knight from every calculation, and captures that looked safe stop being safe.

forkOf.lineName: Four Knights Game / Scotch Four Knights: 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4

notes.explains: The knight comes to c6 covering d4 and adds a second developed piece while the enemy queen has moved three times and holds nothing. Chasing it directly would cost time of your own; this keeps every move useful, and the queen still has to find somewhere to stand.
notes.teaches: Against an early queen sortie, develop at the centre rather than hunting the queen. Every piece that comes out with a job keeps the queen short of safe squares by itself, and the side that spent its opening moves on one piece falls behind while you are simply playing chess.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to d5 and attacks the bishop on c4 while claiming the centre, so the bishop has to spend a move retreating and the centre gets built for free. That is the pattern to look for whenever an enemy piece has been posted on a diagonal a pawn can reach.
notes.teaches: The best central pawn move is the one that arrives hitting something. Building the centre and gaining a move are usually treated as separate goals, and when a single push does both, it is nearly always the move.

notes.explains: The bishop checked and has now stepped back, having achieved one thing: a black piece stands on d7. That square sits between the queen and the pawn on d5, so the queen can no longer take it back — only the knight can. White has spent two moves with the same bishop and still comes out ahead, because the interposition is permanent and the retreat costs nothing.
notes.teaches: A check is worth playing when the only ways to answer it all cost the defender something, even if you intend to retreat straight afterwards. Forcing a piece onto a square where it blocks its own side's plans buys a concession that no amount of quiet development would have obtained.
notes.structural: the interposition is permanent — its checkable claim belongs to Bd7, not to the retreat it is anchored on

notes.explains: Blocking on d7 with the bishop is the natural-looking answer and it quietly costs Black the recapture. The bishop now stands between the queen on d8 and the pawn on d5, so the queen can no longer reach it and Black has to win the pawn back with the knight instead. It also takes d7 from the knight on b8, which now has to settle for c6 or a6.
notes.teaches: A check is worth playing when every legal answer to it costs something. Look at what each reply does to the defender's own pieces before judging the check as slow — the value is not in the check, it is in the awkward square the opponent has to commit to.

notes.opening: Neo-Grünfeld Defense: Classical Variation, Modern Defense
notes.explains: Both sides have finished the same quiet development, and this is the move that decides which game gets played. The pawn arriving on d5 covers c4 and e4 together, so the natural pawn breaks are answered before they are played. The modest alternative one square shorter leaves both of those squares free and invites a bigger centre instead.
notes.teaches: When a setup gives you a free choice of central pawn move, pick the one that takes squares away from the opponent rather than the one that only makes room for you. A pawn on the fourth rank of the centre contests two squares at once, and those are usually the two the other side wanted.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The pawn has stepped to f6 to push the bishop off the diagonal, and the bishop drops back to e3, where it hits the pawn on c5 and covers d4. The pawn move that chased it cannot be taken back, and the squares it gave up are exactly the ones the bishop now works on.
notes.teaches: A bishop chased by a pawn should retreat onto a diagonal that already has a target. If the defender's pawn move to drive you away also weakened a square you can now hit, the retreat has cost nothing and the weakness is permanent.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The bishop steps to h6 and offers itself for the bishop on g7, which is the only piece holding the dark squares near the king. It is defended by the queen behind it, so the offer is real. Declining leaves the bishop sitting on the king's doorstep; accepting hands over the squares the fianchetto was built to hold.
notes.teaches: Against a fianchettoed king, put your bishop where it offers a trade the defender cannot sensibly refuse. Once the guard of the dark squares comes off, every square around the king that a pawn does not cover belongs to the attacker — and the pawns there can never cover them again.

notes.explains: Black has shut the king's bishop in with the d-pawn, and White has developed the light-squared bishop and the queen's knight before touching the centre. The central push is still coming and the game usually transposes to the same structures; the value of holding it back is that it arrives when the pieces are already placed to meet the reply.
notes.teaches: A move order can be worth more than the move it delays. Playing the natural central break a little later, after the pieces are out, keeps the same position available while denying the opponent the setup they have prepared against — and a defender who is not on familiar ground is worth a tempo on its own.
notes.structural: a move-order judgement: the same position reached with the pieces already placed

notes.explains: Black has castled and everything looks routine, but taking on e4 here works: after the recapture the d-pawn comes forward and attacks the knight on e4 and the bishop on c4 together. Dropping the bishop to d3 keeps the bishop pair and the material is level — what is gone is the centre, and trading the e4 pawn for the pawn on d6 is a poor bargain, because it frees the very bishop Black's opening had shut in.
notes.teaches: Whenever a bishop sits on c4 and a pawn on e4 with a knight able to reach it, check for the centre fork trick before you castle: the knight takes the pawn, and after the recapture a pawn advance hits knight and bishop at once. It is not usually winning, but it solves the defender's problems, and that is the point — the cost is paid in structure, not material.
notes.structural: names a resource to check for before castling, not a claim about castling

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: Both obvious recaptures on d4 invite the queen's knight to c6, attacking the piece that just landed there and developing at the same time. Placing the bishop on d3 instead ignores the pawn for now and gets on with the kingside, trusting that d4 is weak enough to collect in due course.
notes.teaches: A pawn taken from you is not a pawn you must take back immediately. When every natural recapture can be hit with tempo, the move that wins the pawn is the one you play later, after the pieces are out — recovering material on the opponent's schedule is how a lead in development gets spent for nothing.

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: The pawn on e5 covers both f6 and d6, so the king's knight and the dark-squared bishop lose their natural developing squares, and Black's position is cut in two with the queenside pieces struggling to join the kingside. That is why White is content to leave d4 alone for the moment: the clamp is worth more than the pawn.
notes.teaches: One advanced pawn can do the work of a piece when it takes away the squares the opponent's pieces most want. Judge such a pawn by what it denies rather than by whether it is defended — and be correspondingly unwilling to part with it.
notes.structural: what the e5 pawn denies — a property of the structure, not of the move played

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: The pawn chain is fixed and White has castled. Three tries come into consideration: the knight to e7, heading for f5 or g6 behind the chain; the bishop out to c5 where it eyes the centre immediately; or the pawn to f6, striking at the head of the chain before the pieces are settled.
notes.teaches: With the centre locked and the king still to be tucked away, the choice is which piece the position needs first. A knight developed behind its own pawns keeps every option; a bishop posted actively commits it; a pawn break at the head of the chain changes the structure at once. All three are played here, and they are not the same game.

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: Black challenges the e5 pawn directly, and the reply is the bishop to b5 — pinning the knight on c6 against the king, since d7 is empty. That takes the sting out of capturing on e5, because recapturing with the knight then hits c6 a second time, from the other side of the board.
notes.teaches: A move that is wrong early can be exactly right once the position has changed. Striking at a cramping pawn with the f-pawn loosens the squares around your own king, so before you play it, ask which enemy piece is waiting to use them.

notes.explains: The bishop has stepped to b4 to swap itself for the knight on c3. The reply is to develop the other bishop to d3, and if the exchange comes, recapturing with the c-pawn is the point — it takes the central squares and opens a path for the queen along the c-file, leaving White the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Being pinned against nothing is not a threat. When a bishop comes out to trade itself for a knight, ask what it actually costs you: doubled pawns are only a weakness if they cannot be used, and a pair of bishops plus open lines is usually the better half of that bargain.

notes.explains: The knight has landed on e5, and from here the choice is between castling and bringing the queen’s knight to d7. The difference matters: the knight on d7 can offer a trade on e5 and change the structure before White's kingside pawns get going, while castling leaves the centre alone and lets the storm start at once.
notes.teaches: A knight planted in the centre is often preparation for a pawn advance elsewhere, not an end in itself. Whether that advance works usually turns on move order — if the opponent can challenge the knight first, the whole plan arrives a move too late.

notes.explains: The advance of the g-pawn drives the bishop, and after it steps to g6 the h-pawn comes too, threatening to push again. Every square the bishop can then reach is covered by a white pawn, so it can only come off for a pawn — which is why the alternative here was the quieter bishop to d3, inviting the trade on White's terms instead.
notes.teaches: Pawns hunt bishops. When your king is castled on the side an enemy pawn storm is coming, count the squares your loose bishop can retreat to and check whether pawns cover them — a bishop with only defended squares to run to is still lost if every one of them can be taken by a pawn.

notes.explains: The centre has just been clarified and both sides look alike. Developing the queen's knight to c6 is the natural move and is the inaccuracy here, because the knight can be harried from b5; the small pawn move to a6 takes the square away first, and it is that line that holds the balance.
notes.teaches: In a symmetrical-looking position the most natural developing move and the move that actually equalises are frequently not the same. Where a knight would be hit by a knight jumping to b5, a quiet pawn move that takes that square away can be worth more than a tempo of development.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: McDonnell Attack, Tal Gambit
notes.explains: The bishop has been given up for the pawn on f7 and the king has taken. White now brings the knight out to f3, which is the only developing move with tempo available, covering e5 and g5 and holding the back rank. From here the attack has one piece out and a bishop invested — the material is not coming back unless the defender helps.
notes.teaches: When a sacrifice on f7 has dragged your king out and there is no follow-up check, the refutation is development, not evasion. Count the attacker's pieces: if only one of them is out, every move you spend bringing a piece toward the king is worth more than the pawn you are up, and the attack runs out before it starts.

notes.explains: Two paths diverge here. Capturing on b2 wins a pawn, but the rook then comes to b1 attacking the queen, and at that moment the only black piece off the back rank besides the queen is the fianchettoed bishop. Advancing in the centre with the d-pawn instead keeps the pieces at home for now but leaves nothing loose.
notes.teaches: Taking the pawn on b2 with the queen is a decision about time, not about material. The rook that swings to b1 arrives with a threat and gains the move it would otherwise have spent developing, so the side that grabbed the pawn ends up defending in a position where nothing else is out.

notes.explains: White has given up a bishop to open lines against the uncastled king, and the black queen sits on a2 with almost nothing else developed. Three tries come into consideration: the knight check, castling, and a quiet queen move — the difference between them is whether they hurry the queen along or shut her escape route first.
notes.teaches: When an enemy queen has raided deep into your position, the move that wins is rarely the check that chases her. Look instead for the quiet move that removes her last route home — a queen with plenty of squares and no way back is a piece you can hunt at leisure.

notes.explains: White has supported the e4 pawn with the f-pawn rather than a piece, so the centre will not disappear on its own. Four continuations branch from here — capturing on e4, developing the queen to b6, bringing the knight round via h6, and striking with the e-pawn — and they lead to genuinely different games rather than transposing.
notes.teaches: Against a big pawn centre propped up by f3, the choice is between resolving the tension at once and keeping it. Releasing it hands the opponent a clear structure to play against; keeping it means accepting a cramped position for a while in exchange for keeping options.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The bishop steps to f4 and looks straight down at the pawn on c7 while covering e5, the square in the middle that both sides want for a knight. It also holds h2, which matters later once the pawns start moving on that wing. Nothing is committed in the centre yet, and the piece that would have been trapped is already out.
notes.teaches: Against a fianchetto, get the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before you build it. Once the modest e-pawn move goes in, that bishop has no way out — so develop it first, on the diagonal where it already has a target, and let the pawns follow.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The centre is closed enough that the game will be decided on a wing, and the pawn goes to h4 covering g5. Black must either let it come to h5 or stop it with the h-pawn, and both replies loosen something around the king. Nothing is threatened for several moves; the point is that the shelter is now a little worse whatever happens.
notes.teaches: A rook's pawn pushed at a fianchettoed king is not an attack yet — it is a question the defender has to answer with a pawn move of their own. Whichever answer comes, a pawn in front of the castled king will have moved, and that is what you were buying.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The knight comes to e5 in the centre, where it hits the pawns on c6, f7 and g6 at the same time. It cannot be taken by a pawn and it cannot be chased by one either, so the only way to remove it is a trade — and every trade there opens a line toward the king the pawns have already been loosened around.
notes.teaches: An outpost is worth more the more it touches. Before planting a knight in the middle, count the pawns it will hit from there — a knight attacking three of them at once cannot simply be ignored, and driving it away usually costs the defender a concession somewhere else.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The pawn goes to f3 and covers e4 and g4, the two squares from which a black knight could come and challenge the outpost. Nothing is attacked and nothing is developed. What has changed is that the knight on e5 now has no way of being asked to leave, so every plan built around it stays available.
notes.teaches: When a knight is doing all the work in the centre, spend a move making sure it cannot be dislodged. A modest pawn move that covers the two squares an enemy knight would jump to is not slow — it is what turns a good square into a permanent one.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The knight has been exchanged and the bishop takes back on e5. From there it hits the knight on f6, which is the piece defending the fianchetto, and it holds the pawn on d4 behind it. The square that was strong for the knight is strong for the bishop as well — and the bishop stares straight at the king.
notes.teaches: When your outpost knight gets traded, recapture with the piece that inherits the square. A bishop that lands on the long diagonal facing a fianchettoed king has taken over the job, and it arrives hitting a piece, so the defender does not get the quiet move the exchange was supposed to win.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The bishop is heading for g7 and the long diagonal. Three continuations come into consideration: developing the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain while it still can get out, mirroring with a fianchetto of your own, or bringing the queen's knight out and leaving the pawns uncommitted for one more move.
notes.teaches: Against a kingside fianchetto the third move decides which structure you are playing for, and all three tries here are sound. The bishop out early claims the dark squares before the pawns commit. The fianchetto answers the opponent on their own terms. The knight out keeps the centre pawns free to advance later. Pick the structure you know.

notes.explains: The bishop has been placed on b7 aiming down the long diagonal at the pawn on e4. Putting the bishop on d3 defends that pawn and the one on c2 behind it, so the whole idea of the setup opposite has nothing to work on. The bishop is modestly placed and it is the move that makes the big centre permanent.
notes.teaches: When the opponent fianchettoes on the queenside, their bishop's only target is your centre pawn. Develop the bishop that defends it rather than the one that looks more active — a centre that cannot be undermined leaves the fianchettoed bishop staring at a wall for the rest of the game.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to e5, hitting the knight on f6 and covering d6. The knight has no comfortable square and the pawn now blocks the long diagonal the bishop on b7 was placed for. One move gains space, gains a tempo, and shuts the opponent's best piece out of the game.
notes.teaches: Space gained with tempo is the cheapest kind. When the centre pawn can advance hitting a knight, look at what the pawn covers once it has moved — if it also takes the square that knight would retreat to, the defender has to find somewhere awkward and the diagonal you were worried about closes at the same time.

notes.explains: Both knights are developed and the g-pawn steps forward to put the bishop on the long diagonal rather than on the usual c4 or b5 square. Nothing is committed yet in the centre: the plan waits to see which setup Black chooses, because the pawn structure Black picks decides where White's pieces belong.
notes.teaches: A fianchetto is unusual in the open game, and that is most of its value at club level: the resulting positions are sound but unfamiliar, so the opponent is out of book while nothing has been risked. It is reachable through more than one move order, which makes it hard to sidestep — the knights can come out in either order before the g-pawn moves.
notes.structural: why an unusual-but-sound setup is worth playing at club level

notes.explains: Both sides have developed symmetrically and nothing is resolved. One try takes on the centre at once. The other steps the g-pawn forward so the bishop can take the long diagonal, keeping the centre closed and asking the opponent to think rather than recite.
notes.teaches: With four knights out and the centre untouched, the fourth move picks the whole character of the game. The central push opens lines immediately and heads for the positions both sides have studied. The fianchetto is unusual in an open game and that is most of its value at club level — sound, and unfamiliar to the person opposite.

notes.explains: The knight arriving on f6 hits the pawn on e4, so the choice is not between developing and attacking — the move does both. That matters most against a set-up that has not committed its centre yet, because the question has to be answered before anything else gets built.
notes.teaches: Given two developing moves, prefer the one that asks a question. A piece that comes out attacking something forces a reply, so you get the tempo to finish developing instead of spending it answering.

notes.explains: Pushing the pawn to e5 hits the knight, and the two pawns covering f6 do not rescue it: taking on f6 would win a piece for a pawn and the recapture only gets the pawn back. So the knight cannot simply sit there, which is exactly what the push is asking. The answer has to be a move that creates a threat of its own rather than a quiet retreat.
notes.teaches: When a pawn attacks a piece, counting defenders is the wrong calculation. The pawn is worth less than anything it hits, so the trade is good for the attacker no matter how many times the square is guarded — the piece has to move, or find a bigger answer elsewhere.

notes.explains: The knight has come to c6 hitting the queen, and instead of retreating she steps sideways to a4, where she hits that same knight back and eyes the pawn on a7. She also holds the pawns on c2 and e4 from there. The move that was supposed to gain time has instead put the knight on a square where it is the piece being asked questions.
notes.teaches: Bringing the queen out early is only bad when she has to move again. Look for the square where the move that chases her has already been made — from there she is out, doing something, and the tempo the opponent expected to win is not available.

notes.explains: The pawn goes to c3 covering b4 and d4, which are the two squares a bishop or knight would use to come at the queen with tempo. It also blunts the fianchettoed bishop's diagonal. Nothing is developed by the move and the position becomes much harder to play against, because the loose piece stops being loose.
notes.teaches: When your queen is out and slightly exposed, the pawn move that covers the squares an enemy piece would use to attack her is worth more than another developing move. Count where the attack could come from, then take those squares away — a queen nobody can hit is simply a developed piece.

notes.explains: The bishop has come to f4 covering the dark squares in the middle. Black can step the knight back and invite the bishop to return, or castle and get on with the game. Both are playable and they lead to completely different results, so this is the moment to know which one you want.
notes.teaches: When a bishop lands on a square the opponent can challenge by shuffling a knight, the position is offering a repetition. Taking it is a legitimate result and refusing it is a decision — but decide, rather than drifting into the same squares three times without noticing what you agreed to.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Smith-Morra Declined
notes.explains: The queen has to choose a square, and the pawn on b2 is hanging. It can be left: the knight that takes it is out of play, and the attack continues with the knight coming to g5 regardless. What matters far more is the pawn on e5, which is the reason the bishop on g7 has nothing to look at — the queen belongs where it keeps that pawn and the attacking pieces together.
notes.teaches: When you are attacking, sort your pawns by what they are doing rather than by whether they can be taken. A pawn that shuts an enemy piece out of the game is part of the attack and must not be traded away to save something else; a pawn on the far side of the board that no piece is using can simply be allowed to fall.

notes.explains: The bishop has taken on f6, which is the whole point of putting it on g5. Both recaptures are legal. Taking with the e-pawn keeps the pawns tidy but leaves the queen's bishop staring at its own pawn. Taking with the g-pawn doubles them on f7 and f6, opens the g-file, and leaves Black with the pair of bishops, since White has just given the dark-squared one away.
notes.teaches: When a bishop takes your knight, the recapture is a choice about what you want the position to look like for the next thirty moves, not a reflex. Taking with the g-pawn accepts doubled pawns and looks ugly; in return it opens a file, keeps both bishops aimed at open diagonals, and leaves the e-pawn free — and doubled pawns that are not weak are simply pawns.

notes.explains: White has closed the position in with the modest e-pawn, and Black's doubled f-pawns are not going anywhere. That makes the c-pawn advance the move the position wants: it strikes at the base of White's centre while the two bishops still have open diagonals to work along.
notes.teaches: A pawn structure tells you which break to look for before any calculation begins. With a solid centre pawn and no dark-squared bishop opposing you, the lever against the queenside is the one that opens lines for the pieces you kept — read the structure, then find the move it asks for.
notes.structural: reads the structure to find the break; one move, so no fork

notes.explains: Black has hit the bishop with the knight and White, instead of retreating it, has pushed the h-pawn. Nothing is hanging and nothing is forced; the position is double-edged and both sides still have everything to play for. Advancing the d-pawn to stake out the centre is the natural, unhurried reply.
notes.teaches: An early rook's-pawn thrust is unsettling rather than refuting. Meet it by asking what it actually does — usually it defends the bishop's retreat square or prepares to open a file — instead of treating strangeness as danger. Being surprised is not the same as being worse.

notes.explains: The bishop is heading for g7 and wants the long diagonal opened. Two tries come into consideration: resolve the centre now, or hold the clamp with the modest pawn move and make the opponent find a way in. Neither is a mistake; they are different bargains.
notes.teaches: With pawns already on c4 and e4 there are two honest plans, and they lead to different games. Pushing the d-pawn two squares opens the centre and hands the fianchettoed bishop the long diagonal it was put there for. Playing it one square keeps everything closed and leaves that bishop biting on granite — quieter, and much harder to play against.

notes.explains: The pawn goes only to d3, where it defends the pawns on c4 and e4 at the same time. Both of those are the clamp — between them they cover the squares in the middle that the opponent's pieces want. Nothing has been grabbed and nothing can be attacked, which is exactly the point.
notes.teaches: A pawn advanced one square instead of two can be the move that makes a whole structure work. Judge it by what it holds rather than by the ground it takes: a single pawn propping up both wings of your centre means neither can be undermined, and a clamp that cannot be broken is worth more than space you have to defend.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to e3, hitting the pawn on c5 and covering d4. That square in the middle is the one the fianchettoed bishop is aimed at through the whole game, and it is now held by a piece that cannot easily be driven away. The centre stays closed and the dark squares stop being available.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has fianchettoed, the fight is for the dark squares that bishop wants to use. Develop the bishop that contests them, and prefer the square where it both holds the central outpost and asks a question of a pawn — a developing move that also denies a square is doing two jobs.

notes.explains: The bishop has been exchanged on f3 and the other bishop takes back. From f3 it holds the pawn on e4, which is half the clamp, and covers g2 and the queen behind it. The knight that guarded those squares is gone and nothing has been loosened, so the trade costs nothing in a position that will not open.
notes.teaches: Giving up a knight for a bishop is not automatically a concession when the position is closed. What matters is whether the recapturing piece takes over the jobs the knight was doing — a bishop that lands defending the centre pawn and the squares around its own king has replaced the knight, not merely traded with it.

notes.explains: The knight has come to e7 and the bishop steps to g5, looking at it with the queen standing behind on d8. The knight still has four legal squares and every one of them loses the queen, so in practice it cannot move at all. The bishop covers f6 and h6 from the same square, which are the squares in front of the fianchetto — so the piece is doing the pinning and the restraining together.
notes.teaches: A piece is pinned in the way that matters whenever every square it can legally reach costs you something behind it. Do not look only for pins against the king: a bishop dropped on the diagonal in front of the queen fixes the piece in between just as firmly, and the defender usually has to spend a pawn move to break it.

notes.explains: The knight has been placed on c6 rather than behind the c-pawn, and the pawn advances to d5 hitting it and the pawn on e6 at the same time. The knight has to jump somewhere awkward or the centre gets opened on terms the developed side chooses. This is the cost of that knight placement, and it arrives the moment the centre is ready.
notes.teaches: When a knight is developed in front of its own c-pawn, the centre push arrives hitting the knight and a pawn together. Before advancing, check whether the defender can answer both — if one reply saves the knight and a different one saves the pawn, the push wins something whatever they choose.

notes.explains: With the pawns locked on d5 and e5, the white centre rests on d4, and the pawn arriving on c5 hits exactly that square. The head of the chain on e5 cannot be attacked profitably while it is defended from behind, so play goes after the pawn holding it up instead.
notes.teaches: A pawn chain is attacked at its base, not at its head. The front pawn is defended by the one behind it, so hitting the rear pawn is the move that asks a real question — take the base away and everything in front of it is loose.

notes.explains: Before this the base on d4 was held only by the queen, which is a defender you would rather not commit so early. The modest pawn move gives d4 a second guard that nothing can harass, so the centre holds and the pieces stay free to develop where they want to go.
notes.teaches: When the base of your chain is attacked, add a pawn defender before you add a piece one. A pawn holds the square without being driven off, while a piece tied to defence has to keep standing there and can be chased.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The knight on b5 threatens to jump into c7, forking the king and the rook in the corner, so the square has to be covered. Bringing the bishop to d6 does cover it, and looks natural because it develops at the same time — but the bishop on c4 then hits the queen on d5 and White gains the move. The knight to a6 covers c7 just as well and asks nothing of the queen.
notes.teaches: When a knight arrives on b5 and eyes c7, that square wants a knight to guard it rather than a bishop. The question is not simply whether a move defends, but whether the defender then becomes a target itself — a guard that can be attacked with tempo has solved one problem by creating another.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The knight has stepped to a3 and is heading for c4, where it would press on b6 and d6. Three replies deal with it: a pawn to a6 preparing to gain space on the queenside, releasing the tension in the centre at once, and developing the queen's knight. The first keeps the most options, because once the white knight reaches c4 the queen's knight comes to d7 to cover b6 while developing, and the b-pawn then evicts the knight and opens the long diagonal for the light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: A knight travelling to the edge is usually going somewhere better, and the reply that keeps most in hand is one that guards the squares it wants while a piece comes into play. Answering a manoeuvre with a manoeuvre keeps the pieces flowing; answering it with pawn moves alone leaves them at home.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The queen can win the pawn on g2 from here, but the bishop then comes to f3 and every white piece arrives with a threat while the queen looks for somewhere to stand. Advancing the e-pawn instead offers the queen trade and keeps everything sound, leaving White only a small pull.
notes.teaches: The pawn on g2 is the most expensive free pawn in the opening. Taking it drags the queen to the edge of the board and away from everything she was doing, and the bill arrives as lost time rather than lost material — which is exactly the currency that decides an opening.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: Two checks are available and only one works. The bishop check on b5 is the eye-catching one, and it is met by interposing the knight on c6. Taking on f7 instead forces the king out, and after the recapture the knight springs to g5 with check: the king has three squares, and the queen on e4 is undefended after every one of them.
notes.teaches: With the enemy queen sitting in the centre and the king still on its starting square, look for the check that wins the queen after the king moves — not the one that looks most like mate. The showy check is usually the one that can simply be blocked; the blunt capture is the one that sets up the fork.

notes.explains: The knight comes to c3 and attacks the pawn on e4, which nothing guards. So the pawn returns and the position that remains is the point of the whole idea: lines are open, development is ahead, and the side that grabbed the pawn has spent two moves on it. Declining to hurry the recapture is also possible, because the pawn is not going anywhere.
notes.teaches: A gambit is only a real sacrifice if the pawn cannot be recovered. Check whether the captured pawn has a defender before treating the material as won — a pawn sitting undefended on an open file is a loan, not a gift.

notes.explains: The bishop arriving on c4 joins the knight in hitting f7, and the only piece covering that square is the king. That is the arithmetic the opening has been working towards since the f-pawn left, and it arrives while the defending side still has pieces on their starting squares.
notes.teaches: Count attackers and defenders on the weak square before calculating anything concrete. When a square next to the king is hit twice and guarded only by the king itself, the tactics are usually already there — the calculation confirms the count rather than discovering it.

notes.explains: The pawn comes to c4 and covers b5 and d5. The central break to d5 is the move this defence uses to free itself, and it is now met by a pawn rather than a piece. Nothing is attacked; the position becomes one where the defender has space to hold and no lever to open it with.
notes.teaches: The way to take a freeing pawn break off the board is to cover its landing square with a pawn of your own. A second pawn on the fourth rank looks like a slow space-grab and is really prophylaxis: the break the defender's whole setup is built around simply stops existing.

forkOf.lineName: Sicilian: Dragon / Accelerated Dragon: Maróczy with ...Qb6

notes.explains: The knights have come off in the centre and the queen takes back. From d4 she hits the knight on f6 and the pawns on a7 and d7, while holding the pawns of the clamp behind her. The exchange that was supposed to relieve the cramped side has instead put the queen on the strongest square on the board.
notes.teaches: Trading knights in a clamped position helps the side with less space, so recapture with the piece that makes the trade cost something. A queen that lands hitting a knight and two pawns at once means the simplification the defender wanted has handed over three tempi instead.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Belgrade Gambit
notes.explains: Black is a pawn up on d4 and the knight on c6 is what holds it. Two bishop developments come into consideration: one to d3, intending to swing round afterwards, and one straight to b5, which attacks the guard at once — once that knight is dealt with, both the knight and the queen are ready to collect on d4.
notes.teaches: To win back a gambit pawn, attack the piece defending it rather than the pawn itself. Counting defenders first tells you which piece to harass, and a bishop that pins or hits the guard does more than a piece aimed at the pawn ever will.

forkOf.lineName: Four Knights Game / Belgrade Gambit: 4.d4 exd4 5.Nd5

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The bishop has been traded for the knight and the pawn recaptures toward the centre. From c6 that pawn covers b5 and d5 — the outpost square in the middle and the square on the wing where a bishop or knight would otherwise sit and annoy. The pawns look untidy on the c-file and the position is perfectly sound, because the squares that matter are held.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are only weak when they cover nothing. Before recapturing, look at which squares each pawn would hold from its new file: a doubled pawn that takes away the two squares the opponent's pieces most want to use has already paid for the cosmetic damage to the structure.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The pawn steps only to d3 rather than to d4. It props up the pawn on e4 so the centre cannot be undermined, and covers c4 so no piece drops in there. The position stays closed while the pieces come out — which is exactly what the side without the bishop pair wants.
notes.teaches: When you have given up the bishop pair, do not rush to open the position. The modest one-square pawn move keeps the centre closed enough that the two bishops have nothing to aim at, and time spent making the position solid is time the opponent cannot spend making it sharp.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The bishop has been traded on f3 and the queen takes back. From f3 she hits the knight on f6 immediately, so the recapture comes with a question attached rather than as a pause. She also stands behind the pawns on d3, e4, g2 and h3, which means there is no square from which she can be harassed.
notes.teaches: When two pieces can recapture, take with the one that lands doing something. A queen that arrives hitting a piece has gained the move the recapture would normally cost, and if she also sits behind her own pawns she is safe from being chased off again.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The centre is locked with pawns on e4 and e5 and neither side can force it open there. The pawn goes to a4 and covers b5, which is the square the queenside pawn break needs. With that square held, the position has no natural way to be opened, and the game becomes about who can improve their worst piece.
notes.teaches: In a closed position the pawn breaks are the only way in, so the strongest prophylactic move is often the one that takes a break square away before the break is prepared. A pawn spent on the wing costs nothing here — nothing is happening quickly, and the plan it stops was the opponent's only one.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: With the pawns fixed, the knight on c3 has nothing left to do there. Dropping back to e2 keeps it covering d4, the one central square either side could use as an outpost, and opens the route toward the kingside where the position is not yet decided. Retreating is not passive when the square behind is a crossroads.
notes.teaches: In a locked position a knight that has run out of squares should retreat toward a route rather than stand still. Judge the retreat by where it can go next and by what it holds on the way — a knight stepping back while still covering the key central square has lost nothing at all.

notes.explains: The pawn push has been taken and the bishop recaptures on c4, back on the diagonal pointing at f7. The centre pawns have come off, so nothing blocks it any more, and the king opposite has not yet castled. The structure is now symmetrical and the position is not — one bishop is aimed at a target and the other is not.
notes.teaches: Offering a pawn trade to reopen your own bishop's diagonal is a fair bargain when the pawn comes straight back. Count what the bishop is aiming at after the recapture rather than what the structure looks like — a bishop restored to the long light diagonal with the king still in the centre is worth the simplification.

notes.explains: The pawn has been offered on c5 and the centre pawn advances past it to d5, covering c6 and e6. Those are the squares the knight and the light-squared bishop want. The position locks, which suits the side whose bishop is already outside the pawn chain — the piece that could have been trapped is the one with the open diagonal.
notes.teaches: When the bishop comes out before the pawns are settled, a pawn push in the centre answers the challenge by closing it. Judge the push by the two squares it covers rather than by the space it takes: with both entry squares held by a pawn, the pieces opposite have nowhere to develop toward and the bishop outside the chain is safe.

notes.explains: The pawn has come to e5 to hit the bishop, and the bishop drops back to g3 still looking at that same pawn. It also holds the pawns on f2 and h2 behind it. The advance gained space and created a target in the same move, and the bishop is now the piece asking the questions.
notes.teaches: A bishop attacked by a pawn advance should retreat along the diagonal rather than off it, if the square behind still bears on the pawn that just moved. The pawn cannot come back, so the retreat keeps the target and the tempo the opponent spent is gone.

notes.explains: The pawn has advanced to e5 to chase the queen out of the centre. She steps to b4, where she hits the pawns on b7 and d6 and still holds the centre pawn and the knight behind her. The move that was meant to gain time has instead pointed her at the two pawns the pawn advance left behind.
notes.teaches: A queen driven off a central square should look for the diagonal that hits two pawns at once rather than the nearest safe square. When both targets are on squares a pawn can never defend, the defender has to answer with a piece, and the queen has kept the initiative she was supposed to lose.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to e5 and asks the question directly, attacking d4 while nothing yet defends the position properly. Waiting one move to develop first would let that centre be reinforced, and then the same break arrives against a set-up that is ready for it.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has spent moves building a broad centre with pawns, hit it before the pieces arrive to support it. A centre that has to be defended by pieces is a liability; the same centre given a free move to consolidate becomes a space advantage.

notes.explains: Taking on e5 here loses the pawn straight back: the queen checks from h4 and the pawn on e4 has no defender at all, so it drops with tempo. Developing the knight to f3 covers h4 instead, which does not make the queen sortie illegal but does make it cost a queen for a knight. Material can wait; the check square cannot.
notes.teaches: Before taking a pawn in the centre, look for the check that comes with it. A queen check on the edge of the board is easy to dismiss as a lunge, but if it arrives with tempo and collects a loose pawn on the way back, the capture was never free.

notes.explains: Black jumps the knight to d4 instead of defending, offering the trade in the centre and inviting the bishop to declare itself. Three replies branch here: taking on d4, retreating the bishop along the diagonal, and dropping it all the way home. The resulting pawn structures do not arise from any other line in this opening.
notes.teaches: Some sidelines are not shortcuts into the main lines — they build a structure that appears nowhere else in the opening. When a line does that, general familiarity with the parent opening will not carry you, and the only preparation that helps is knowing this position specifically.

notes.explains: White has taken on d4 and castled, leaving Black a pawn on d4 and a choice. Two moves are genuinely playable: the bishop to c5, which is the most common, and the modest c6, taking the b5 square away. Anything else concedes more than the line can afford.
notes.teaches: An opening the books call dubious is only dubious against an accurate reply. That is exactly why strong players still pick one — the objective verdict matters less than whether the person opposite has looked at it recently.

notes.explains: The bishop has come to c4 and now eyes f7. Taking there with check drags the king out, and the queen arriving on h5 forces a pawn move — after which the undefended bishop on c5 falls. That is the tactical point behind the natural-looking bishop move, and it is why Black's replies here all have to reckon with it.
notes.teaches: A bishop aimed at f7 combines with a queen that can reach h5, and the two together are worth more than either alone. Before developing a bishop where it can be hit by that pair, check whether it is defended — the check on f7 is only the setup, and the piece it wins is somewhere else entirely.

notes.explains: The knight has just come to f6, and pushing the e-pawn attacks it immediately. Black cannot meet it by striking back in the centre, because that opens lines toward the king while the pieces are still at home; the pawn has to come forward first, and only then can the position be held together.
notes.teaches: When a knight develops to its natural square in front of a pawn that can advance, the advance usually comes with tempo — and a tempo spent chasing a piece is a tempo you did not have to spend on development. Look for the pawn push before you look for a new piece to move.

notes.explains: Both knights and the dark-squared bishop are developed and Black has struck at the centre from the side. The pawn advances to e4 hitting the pawn on d5 and covering f5. Taking it leads to a position where every white piece has a line and the extra pawn is on a square that cannot be held.
notes.teaches: A gambit is worth playing when the pawn buys development you were going to need anyway. Pushing the second centre pawn while both minor pieces are already out hits the pawn holding the centre and opens the line for the pieces behind it — the material comes back or it does not, but the position opens for the side that is ready.

notes.explains: The pawns have been traded in the centre and there are two ways to continue. Taking back restores material immediately and asks nothing. Jumping the knight to b5 instead hits the weak pawn the setup opposite created, and the pawn in the middle can be collected a move later.
notes.teaches: When the centre opens, recapturing is the move you play if nothing better exists — so look for the jump first. A knight that lands hitting several pawns at once cannot be answered by defending one of them, and the pawn in the middle is usually still there afterwards.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to e3, where it holds the knight in the centre and covers the squares in front of it. The fianchettoed bishop on g7 is aimed down the long diagonal at that knight, and this quietly answers it — the knight is no longer loose, so the pawn breaks that would have won it are simply moves.
notes.teaches: Against a fianchetto the dark-squared bishop belongs where it both supports your own centre and contests the diagonal the enemy bishop was put on. A developing move that defends the piece already in the middle costs nothing and removes every tactic built on hitting it.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to f3, defending the pawn on e4 and covering g4 so no bishop or knight can land there. That single move is what makes the whole setup work: the centre cannot be undermined, the kingside pawns are free to advance, and the king has somewhere to go on the other wing.
notes.teaches: Before castling on the side you intend to attack, spend the pawn move that makes the attack legal. Holding the centre pawn and covering the square an enemy piece would use to come forward is what lets the king go the other way and the pawns march — without it, the attack is a plan the position cannot support.

notes.explains: The knights have come off in the centre and the bishop steps to d4, straight down the long diagonal at the bishop on g7. It hits the pawn on a7 on the way and holds the knight on c3 behind it. The defender must either accept the exchange of the king's best guard or spend moves avoiding it while the pawns are already coming.
notes.teaches: When attacking a fianchettoed king, the piece to remove is the bishop on the long diagonal — it is the only defender that covers the dark squares around the king. Getting your own bishop onto the same diagonal facing it forces the trade or forces the king's guard to stay home, and either answer helps the attack.

notes.explains: The knight covers e4, so the pawn is ready to come there next and take the whole centre. That is the threat this move order lives on: an answer that ignores it lets the big centre appear and hands the opponent a game they chose rather than one you did. Meeting it in the centre keeps that push honest, because the pawn arriving on e4 can then simply be taken.
notes.teaches: When a knight develops before the centre pawns, look at which pawn break it has just made possible. A quiet-looking developing move can be the one that decides whether your opponent gets to choose their own opening or gets steered into yours.

notes.explains: Once the pawn arrives on h5 the white h-pawn has nowhere to go: its one square is occupied and it cannot capture, so the pawn storm stops without a piece being touched. That is why the attacking side treats this as the main line and starts looking at sacrificing on h5 instead — the pawn alone can no longer make progress.
notes.teaches: Against a rook pawn running at a fianchetto, meeting it head on is the move that ends the discussion. A pawn that has been blocked on an open file is not slow — it has no squares at all, and the attacker has to find a different plan or spend pieces.

notes.explains: Stepping the queen to d2 empties the last square between king and queen's rook, so castling long becomes available. That is the side the king belongs on here, because the h-pawn has already committed to the attack and going short would put the king behind it. The queen also connects to the bishop on f4, so the move does two jobs.
notes.teaches: A quiet queen move is often a castling move. Before reading a developing move as slow, check which squares it empties — the last piece to leave the back rank is what makes the king's journey to the other wing possible.

notes.explains: The pawn on c3 invites the capture, and taking it opens the diagonals the whole attack is built on. The other try ignores the offer and strikes in the centre instead, returning the pawn on terms you choose rather than on terms your opponent has prepared for.
notes.teaches: A gambit pawn offered a second time is a question about time, not about greed. You can take everything and spend the next ten moves untangling, or hand one pawn straight back in the centre and reach a position where the extra material was never the point. Both are playable; only one of them lets you decide what the game looks like.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to d5 and hits the pawn on e4, so the centre has to be resolved immediately rather than at leisure. It also covers c4, which is where the light-squared bishop wants to sit and stare at f7. Giving the pawn back here buys both of those, and the attack loses the square it was built around.
notes.teaches: The best way to decline a gambit is usually a pawn move that does two jobs at once. Look for the push that hits something and takes away the square the attacking piece was heading for — a defender that gains a move while removing a plan is worth more than a pawn.

notes.explains: Both bishops are now on their diagonals. The dark-squared one has taken on b2 and looks straight down at g7, and it covers f6 as well, so the natural developing square for the king's knight is contested before the knight has moved. Nothing is won yet; what has been bought is that every black piece must now come out with the attack already pointing at it.
notes.teaches: Count what a gambit buys in lines, not in pawns. Two pawns given up for two bishops raking toward the same king is a real bargain when the defender still has pieces at home — the moment the position opens, every tempo spent taking is a tempo not spent developing.

notes.explains: The bishop has come to b4 with check and it must be dealt with at once. Four answers are on the board: the king steps to f1, or one of three pieces interposes on the c3 and d2 squares — and each of them changes what the position is about. Blocking with the dark-squared bishop offers a trade of the piece doing the most work.
notes.teaches: When every way of answering a check gives something up, the choice is about which concession you can live with. Blocking with a piece invites a trade you may not want, stepping the king aside forfeits castling, and the bishop that came to block is often the one the whole attack depended on. Pick the concession, do not stumble into it.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to e5 and hits the pawn on d6, so the centre cannot simply be left alone. What matters more is that it now covers f6, so the king's knight has lost its natural square while the position is still open. That is the shape of the whole gambit: not one big threat, but a series of small ones that each cost the defender a move.
notes.teaches: A pawn push in the centre earns its place when it hits a pawn and takes a square from a piece in the same move. Before you push, look at what the pawn will cover once it has moved — the square behind the target is often worth more than the target.

notes.explains: Black has stabilised with the pawn on d6 and the position is level in material after the pawn came back. Four tries come into consideration: two different queen placements, the natural knight development, and the central push. They lead to genuinely different games rather than to a single best line.
notes.teaches: With a lead in development and no forced win, the choice is which piece to commit and how early. A queen sortie asks a question immediately but can be answered by a queen move; a quiet developing move keeps every option and asks nothing. There is no refutation to find here, only a preference to have.

notes.explains: The pawn has been offered on c5 and is taken. From there it covers b6 and d6, which are the two squares a knight or a bishop would use to win it back. Nothing recaptures immediately, so the extra pawn either survives or costs the defender a move to collect while the pieces opposite are still at home.
notes.teaches: Capturing toward the wing looks like it concedes the centre, and the question is what the pawn does from its new square. A pawn on the sixth file that covers both squares the opponent needs to recapture from is not a loose pawn — it is a wedge that has to be dealt with before anything else happens.

notes.explains: The bishops have been traded and the pawn on f4 has committed the attack. The queen steps to e1, where she holds the pawn on e4, connects the pieces on the back rank, and can travel to the kingside along the third rank once the pawns advance. Nothing is attacked yet; the piece that will lead the attack has simply been put where it can join it.
notes.teaches: In a kingside attack the queen usually belongs behind the pawns rather than in front of them. A move to the back rank that clears her original square, holds the centre pawn and opens the route toward the king does three jobs and threatens nothing — which is exactly why it is hard to meet.

notes.explains: Both sides have made modest pawn moves and the position is still closed. The bishop goes to b2 on the long diagonal, where it hits the pawn on e5 and covers d4 — the square the centre would be contested from. It also holds the rook in the corner. Nothing has been risked, and the piece that will decide the game is pointing at the only fixed target on the board.
notes.teaches: A slow setup with pawns on the third rank is answered on its own terms: build the same shape, then develop the bishop onto the diagonal where the opponent's centre pawn already stands. The bishop arrives with a target rather than into empty space, which is the whole difference between a passive system and a patient one.

notes.explains: Two replies divide here. Developing the king's knight is the sound, mainstream choice. Jumping the queen's knight to d4 instead is the tricky one — it exists and is played, but it invites White to take on e5, and from there Black is relying on the opponent going wrong.
notes.teaches: A move can be playable, well known and still not good. Openings collect lines that survive because they set traps rather than because they equalise, and the way to meet one is to know the refutation rather than to avoid the whole position.

notes.explains: Grabbing the pawn on e4 with the knight loses a piece outright — White castles and the knight cannot be held, with the black queen and king sitting on the e-file behind it. The move that works instead is pushing the d-pawn, which cuts across the bishop's diagonal and the knight's path at the same time.
notes.teaches: A queen standing on the same file as her own king is a standing invitation, and it is worth noticing before you go pawn-grabbing rather than after. When the file between them can be opened, the tactics tend to appear on their own.

notes.explains: Taking the rook on h8 is the greedy try, and after Black recaptures the bishop on c4 the knight has just two squares to leave by, g6 and f7, and Black covers them both. The alternative is to take on d5 and keep the pieces in play; the position stays messy, but nothing is stranded.
notes.teaches: A rook in the corner is worth more than a knight only if the knight comes home. Before taking material with a piece that has to travel back through enemy territory, count its exit squares — a won exchange that costs the piece which won it is not won at all.

notes.explains: The knight can leap to c7 with check, hitting the king and the rook in the corner at once — but the queen on f7 travels along the seventh rank and takes it, and the whole idea comes to nothing. Retreating the knight to b6 keeps material, though it leaves the king alone in the centre, where the queen swings to g6 and hunts it down the light squares.
notes.teaches: When you calculate a discovered attack, check that the piece you intend to win cannot simply capture the piece doing the discovering. That single question is what separates a real double attack from one that evaporates, and it is the most common way these tricks are miscounted.

notes.explains: Every white move so far has been a pawn, and the c-pawn takes still more ground while the knight on d5 is asked to move again. It is a real gain and a real risk at once: the knight drops back to b6 or c7 and White has to bring pieces out quickly, because a centre this wide with nothing developed behind it invites a counterstrike.
notes.teaches: Taking a large share of the centre with pawns is not the same as being ahead, and the danger grows with every further pawn move. Grabbing more space while none of your pieces are out is playable only if you can follow it immediately with accurate development — the space has to be defended by something.

notes.explains: Bringing the king's knight to f3 hands the light-squared bishop a job: it comes to g4 and pins the knight against the queen on d1, since e2 is empty. Developing the queen's knight to c3 first leaves f3 vacant, so that bishop has nothing to attack and has to choose a square on its own terms.
notes.teaches: When two knights both want to come out, the order is decided by which one can be given a target. Develop the piece that cannot be harassed first and leave the other at home a moment longer — the opponent then has to commit a piece without knowing what it will be aiming at.

notes.explains: The pawn on f3 supports the centre and blocks the king's knight from its natural square. Three replies come into consideration: capturing in the centre straight away, the modest pawn move that keeps the position closed, or bringing a knight out and leaving the tension for another move.
notes.teaches: When the centre is propped up by a pawn rather than a piece, you can take it, sidestep it, or develop and leave the tension. Taking resolves the position at once and hands over the centre. Sidestepping keeps everything closed and asks whether the prop was worth the move. Developing declines the argument entirely. All three are played here.

notes.explains: White has rebuilt the centre with the pawn on e4 and the f-file is open. Two tries come into consideration: the central pawn push that challenges the pawn head-on, or the king's knight developing onto it, which asks the same question without committing a pawn.
notes.teaches: Against a big centre held by pawns you can strike it or develop at it. The pawn break challenges immediately and accepts an open game; the knight comes out hitting the same pawn and keeps the tension for another move. Which you want depends on whether you are happy to open the position while your king is still at home.

notes.explains: The queen's knight is out and Black has answered symmetrically. Several continuations come into consideration and they lead to genuinely different games: an immediate trade on the queenside, quiet development, a kingside fianchetto, or the pawn storm. There is nothing to refute here.
notes.teaches: Some positions have no best move, only a choice of what kind of game you want. A bishop out to the edge, a knight to its natural square, a fianchetto, a big pawn move on the f-file — each is sound, and each commits you to a different plan. Pick the one you understand rather than the one you half-remember.

notes.explains: The bishop steps to b5 and hits the knight on c6. Black can defend it, block, move it, or ignore the offer and let the trade happen, and each choice fixes something about the pawn structure for the rest of the game. From b5 the bishop also covers c4 and d3, so the light squares in the centre stay contested whatever happens.
notes.teaches: Offering to trade a bishop for a knight early is a structural decision made with a developing move. The knight is the piece holding the defender's centre together, so the offer must be answered — and however it is answered, something has been committed that was not committed a move ago.

notes.explains: The pawns have been traded and the knight takes back in the middle of the board. From there it covers b5, c6, e6 and f5 — the squares a bishop or knight would use to come forward — and holds the pawn on c2 behind it. Nothing is attacked; what has changed is that there is no comfortable square left for the pieces that have not developed yet.
notes.teaches: When you recapture in the centre with a knight, look at the squares it now covers rather than at the ground it occupies. A knight in the middle that holds b5, c6, e6 and f5 has taken over four entry points at once — the defender's pieces have nowhere to land, and that is what a central knight is really for.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation
notes.explains: The expansion with b5 is what this whole set-up is for, but played right now it simply drops a pawn: the c-pawn and the queen's knight both cover b5, and only the pawn on c6 guards it. The rook's pawn to a6 makes it two against two, and from here the break goes in whenever the moment is right rather than never.
notes.teaches: Before pushing a pawn into the opponent's half, count the pieces covering the square it lands on. A break that is one defender short is not a break, it is a donation — and the cheapest repair is almost always a quiet pawn move on the neighbouring file, which costs a tempo and buys the whole plan.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation
notes.explains: The knight arrives on b6 hitting the bishop and joining the pieces already trained on d5. Count where that bishop can go and the position speaks for itself — of its six squares, exactly two keep it guarding the pawn, and both of them are behind it on the same diagonal, further from the game rather than nearer to it.
notes.teaches: When a piece has been reduced to guarding a single pawn, push it further back before it can be re-routed. Time spent harassing a defender is not time lost: every square you take away from it is a square it can never help from again.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation
notes.explains: The pawn steps to c4 and shuts the bishop off the long diagonal it was defending along. Three defenders become two, against three attackers, and the pawn on d5 cannot simply be guarded again: the one move that adds a defender without losing material is the central push, which is exactly the concession being played for.
notes.teaches: A pawn does not have to attack a square to win it. Pushing past a defender cuts the line that defender was working along, and a point held three times by pieces that can no longer see it is a point held twice. Removing a guard and adding an attacker are the same arithmetic from opposite ends.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation
notes.explains: The offer to trade on h6 is coming, and with the rook where it stands the retreat along the diagonal walks into a capture on the square the rook has just left, which means the trade cannot be declined. Stepping the rook to e8 empties that square and the retreat becomes free. It is a piece of technique worth keeping: the rook move looks like ordinary development and is really the answer to a threat one move ahead.
notes.teaches: When the whole character of your position rests on one bishop, look for the move that gives it a safe retreat before it is ever challenged. A fianchettoed bishop offered a trade has only one square to duck to, and whether ducking is possible depends on a rook standing a file away — so move the rook first, while it is still free.
notes.structural: prophylaxis one move ahead of a threat; one move, so no fork

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation
notes.explains: The bishop stands on g7 aiming through the centre. One try puts a bishop opposite it on the same diagonal, so the piece the opponent built around has something to look at. The other develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, where it contests the squares in front of the fianchetto rather than facing it down.
notes.teaches: With both centre pawns out and the opponent fianchettoed, the choice is whether to answer on the long diagonal or on the dark squares. A fianchetto of your own blunts their best piece by facing it; the bishop developed outside the chain contests the squares that bishop wants to use instead. Both are mainstream and they ask different questions.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Maróczy Bind, Gurgenidze Variation
notes.explains: The queen steps out to b6 and takes aim at the pawn on b2, which is the obvious half of the move. The half that makes it work is that the bishop on e3 has no defender, and it is one of the two pieces holding the knight on d4 together. Grabbing material immediately would let the position be defended; asking a second question first is what makes the loose bishop start to matter.
notes.teaches: Before playing the capture you can see, look for the piece that is not defended. A tactic usually fails or succeeds on one loose piece somewhere else on the board, and the strongest move is often the quiet one that adds a second problem while that piece stays loose.

notes.explains: The bishop comes out to c4 aiming at the pawn on f7, the only pawn near the king with no pawn defending it. From the same square it covers d5, which is where the defender's freeing pawn break wants to land, and b5. Nothing is threatened yet; what has happened is that the natural ways to free the position are all a little harder.
notes.teaches: A bishop on c4 is doing more than staring at f7. From that square it also covers d5 and b5 — the two squares the defender needs for a knight or a freeing pawn — so it restrains as much as it attacks. Judge the piece by the whole diagonal, not by the one square at the end of it.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to d3 and defends the bishop on c4 and the pawn on e4 at the same time. Both were the loose points in the position: the bishop could be hit by a pawn coming to d5, and the centre pawn had nothing behind it. One quiet move removes both problems and the position becomes simply solid.
notes.teaches: When a bishop is committed early, spend the modest pawn move that supports it. A single pawn holding both the bishop and the centre pawn means neither can be won by a pawn advance, and the position stops having a tactical answer — which is exactly what an early bishop needs.

notes.explains: The pawn has come to d5 and the bishop must move. Going to b5 hits the knight on c6, which is the piece supporting the centre, so the move that looked forced arrives with a threat. The bishop also holds the pawn on d3 from there, so nothing is left loose behind it.
notes.teaches: When a pawn advance chases your bishop, look for the retreat square that attacks something rather than the one that keeps the old diagonal. A bishop driven backwards has lost time; a bishop driven sideways onto the piece holding the centre has gained it back.

notes.explains: The knight jumps to e5 where it hits the knight on c6 — already attacked by the bishop — and the pawn on f7 at the same time. Defending c6 does nothing about f7 and vice versa, so the defender has to give something up or accept a trade on terms they did not choose. The knight also holds the pawn on d3 behind it.
notes.teaches: Two pieces attacking the same piece is the ordinary way to win it; two pieces attacking two different things is better. Look for the square where the knight joins the bishop against one target and picks up a second one on its own.

notes.explains: Both knights are out and the centre is still unresolved. Three continuations come into consideration here: taking on the centre at once, the bishop to b5 hitting the knight that holds it, or the bishop to c4 aiming at the weakest square near the enemy king. They lead to genuinely different games rather than to a single best line.
notes.teaches: Three sound third moves with little between them objectively, and a real difference in what you are signing up for. Opening the centre leads to the positions both sides have studied hardest. Offering the bishop for the knight trades a piece for a permanent change in the pawn structure. Putting the bishop out toward f7 keeps everything flexible and takes the game somewhere far less familiar — which at club level is most of its value.

notes.explains: The knight on b5 wants to land on c7, where it would check the king and hit the rook in the corner at the same time. Three replies deal with it: a bishop check on b4 that answers the threat by making one of its own, a knight to a6 covering the square from the edge, and a bishop to d6 blocking the square directly. All three address c7; they are not equally good.
notes.teaches: When one square is the whole problem, list every way of dealing with it before choosing — guard it, occupy it, or hit something bigger elsewhere. The move that comes to mind first is usually the one that defends most obviously, and obvious defence and best defence are different things.

notes.explains: Black has just recaptured on d6 with the c-pawn, accepting doubled pawns on the d-file in exchange for the half-open c-file. From here the queen sortie to b6 is the critical try, while castling is the move most players reach for.
notes.teaches: The reply you will actually meet is not always the sharpest one. Preparing only for the critical try leaves you improvising in the position that turns up most often, so it is worth knowing the ordinary continuation at least as well as the forcing one.

notes.explains: The g- and h-pawns are marching at the bishop on g6, and the threat of pushing the h-pawn again is the reason Black is uncomfortable. Stopping it with the h-pawn does not solve the problem either: the knight on e5 simply takes the bishop, and recapturing with the f-pawn wrecks the pawns in front of the king, leaving the pawn on g6 as the next target.
notes.teaches: A bishop developed outside its own pawn chain can be chased by pawns, and the chase costs nothing when your king has not committed to that side. Before placing a bishop where pawns can reach it, look at whether the opponent's kingside pawns are still free to advance.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: Both sides are developed and the tension in the centre still stands. One try is a modest pawn move on the edge that removes a square before it is used. The other takes on c6 immediately, doubling the pawns there and opening a file, which changes what both sides are playing for.
notes.teaches: Against a fianchettoed bishop you can either spend a quiet move keeping the position intact, or resolve the centre at once and accept a structural change in return. The quiet move looks like it does nothing and is preventing something; the exchange gives the defender doubled pawns and gives up the tension. Both are real; they are not the same game.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: The pawn steps to a3 and covers b4, which is the square the queen and the dark-squared bishop both eye when they want to hit the knight on c3 with something behind it. Nothing is threatened and nothing is developed; what has changed is that a whole family of annoying moves is off the board before it appears.
notes.teaches: A pawn move on the edge that develops nothing and attacks nothing can still be the best move on the board. Judge it by the square it takes away: if the piece that wanted that square was going to arrive with tempo, the quiet move has saved the move it would have cost you.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: The bishop comes to c4 and stares at the pawn on f7, which is the only pawn near the king not defended by another pawn. From the same square it covers d5, so the freeing pawn break in the centre is contested before it is played. That double duty is why this square, rather than a more modest one, is the one to aim for. From here two tries come into consideration: grabbing the pawn on e4 with the knight, which looks free because the pawn appears loose and walks into the capture on f7, or the freeing pawn push that contests the centre while the bishop still has nothing to hit.
notes.teaches: A bishop aimed at f7 is doing two jobs whenever the defender has castled: it hits the pawn in front of the king, and it covers the square in the centre that the defender's pieces most want. Before you decide the bishop is only an attacking piece, look at what it holds behind the attack.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: The knight has taken on e4 and there are two ways to answer. Recapturing the knight straight away keeps everything simple. Taking on f7 with check first is the move: the king has to choose between stepping out and letting the rook come to f7, and only then does the knight come off. Material ends up level — what has changed is where the black king lives.
notes.teaches: Given a chance to win back a piece or to take a pawn with check, look at what the check does to the defender's position before assuming the recapture is better. A capture that forces the king to move or drags a rook onto an awkward square buys more than the exchange of pieces it costs.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: Black's pawn stands on c6 with b7 and c7 empty behind it. The pawn advances to e5, hitting the knight on f6, and it covers d6 as well, so the knight cannot drop back into the middle of the position. It has to go somewhere awkward, and every move it spends finding a square is a move the attacker spends developing.
notes.teaches: After trading in the centre, the follow-up push earns its place if it hits a piece and takes a square in one move. The knight it attacks is usually the piece holding the defender's position together, and the square behind the pawn is where the attack wants to land next.

notes.opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Kasparov Attack
notes.explains: Black has recaptured on f6 and the knights are off, leaving a symmetrical-looking centre where Black is solid but short of space. Several setups are available: a kingside fianchetto with the g-pawn, the classical bishop to d3, and the modest c-pawn move, which is easy to read as pure consolidation and is well regarded precisely because it is not.
notes.teaches: Against a defence that is solid rather than sharp, there is nothing to refute — so the opening question stops being which line wins and becomes which setup you want to play. Choose by the kind of position you want on the board, because all of the reasonable tries here are sound and they lead to different games.

notes.opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Kasparov Attack
